content: The metabolism of CYP3A4 is a critical factor in drug interactions involving quinine. Cenobamate reduces the levels or effects of quinine by altering hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy adjustments and close monitoring are recommended, including dose increases of CYP3A4 substrates when co-administered with cenobamate. Quinine increases ceritinib levels via the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter, necessitating caution and monitoring. Both chlorpromazine and quinine prolong the QTc interval, requiring careful observation. Cimetidine elevates quinine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism and competing for renal tubular clearance, warranting caution. Ciprofloxacin and quinine also prolong the QTc interval, though ciprofloxacin has minimal QT effects; caution is advised when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs or in patients with risk factors. Quinine and citalopram both increase the QTc interval, necessitating ECG monitoring and caution with other QT-prolonging drugs. Clarithromycin raises quinine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism and prolongs the QTc interval, requiring close monitoring. Crofelemer increases quinine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 in the gut, though systemic inhibition is unlikely due to minimal absorption. Cyclosporine elevates quinine levels via the P-glycoprotein transporter, requiring caution. Quinine increases dabigatran levels via P-glycoprotein, and co-administration should be avoided in patients with reduced renal function (CrCl <30 mL/min for atrial fibrillation or <50 mL/min for DVT/PE treatment).
